highlights: Al Olaya landmark with golden-sphere dining, polished Arabian interiors and women-only spa rituals
description:
Mandarin Oriental, Riyadh occupies one of the capital’s most prominent addresses in Al Olaya, directly beneath the landmark Al Faisaliah Tower on King Fahad Road. The setting places the hotel at the centre of Riyadh’s business, shopping and cultural momentum, with the redeveloped Faisaliyah Centre’s upscale retail, city restaurants and major commercial districts close at hand.

The hotel has entered the Mandarin Oriental era after a comprehensive renovation, bringing a lighter, more contemporary tone to 226 accommodations and the public spaces around them. Rooms and suites are styled with pale neutrals, polished woods and Arabian accents, while larger residences such as the Royal Suite and Penthouse Suite add expansive living areas, balcony views and a more residential mood.

Dining is unusually broad for a city hotel. The Globe remains the signature address, set inside the golden sphere high above the tower and known for sweeping Riyadh views with a modern European menu. La Brasserie adds an animated international dining room, while LPM Restaurant & Café, Mamo Michelangelo, Yauatcha, The Mandarin Lounge and Asir Lounge broaden the culinary range from French Mediterranean to dim sum, Italian and evening drinks.

Wellness is anchored by Al Faisaliah Spa, a richly detailed women-only sanctuary with hammam rituals, treatment rooms and a sense of retreat from the city. An indoor pool, fitness facilities, meeting spaces and wedding venues complete the offering, giving the property a polished urban profile with one of Riyadh’s most recognisable skylines as its backdrop. Together, these elements make it feel like a composed civic landmark rather than a sealed-off business hotel.

hotel_name: Four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea
highlights: Wailea beachfront glamour with saline pools, Hawaiian art and Lanai-facing sunset views
description:
Four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea sits on the golden crescent of Wailea Beach, on Maui’s sun-soaked southwest coast. From this address, Wailea’s golf, boutiques and resort dining are close by, while Haleakalā National Park, the Road to Hāna and the island’s lava-sculpted shoreline provide a wider sense of place beyond the sand.

The resort is substantial, with 383 rooms and suites arranged in a multi-storey, U-shaped building around gardens, fountains and the oceanfront pool complex. Its refreshed interiors lean into contemporary tropical Hawaiian motifs, private lanais and a collection of Hawaiian art, with many rooms angled toward the Pacific, Lāna‘i, the West Maui Mountains or the resort’s palms and lawns.

Dining ranges from Spago Maui to Ferraro’s Restaurant & Bar, DUO Steak and Seafood and KOMO, the sushi-focused addition shaped by chef Kiyo Ikeda. Poolside drinks, beach dining and private in-suite meals extend the culinary rhythm across the day without turning the resort into a formal grand hotel.

Three saline pools define much of the outdoor life, including the adults-only Serenity Pool with views toward Lāna‘i and the West Maui Mountains. Wailea Beach supports non-motorised ocean activities such as stand-up paddle boarding, snorkelling and outrigger canoeing, while the resort adds fitness, pickleball, golf access, Kids for All Seasons programming and a new Spa & Wellness Centre with aquathermal facilities and treatment spaces. The overall mood is polished, sunny and recognisably Hawaiian, with enough scale for families yet sufficient calm for longer, slower stays. Its fame as the setting for the first season of The White Lotus adds a contemporary cultural footnote without overwhelming the Hawaiian character.

highlights: Adults-only jungle sanctuary of fifteen tented bungalows, Pacific views and ritual-led wellness
description:
Naviva, A Four Seasons Resort is tucked into Punta Mita on Mexico’s Riviera Nayarit, north of Puerto Vallarta and beside the established Four Seasons Resort Punta Mita. The adults-only retreat feels far removed from conventional resort life, occupying 48 acres of coastal forest where jungle paths, Pacific views and the private peninsula’s beaches shape the pace of each day.

The scale is deliberately intimate: just 15 luxury tented bungalows, each conceived as a soft-edged indoor-outdoor hideaway rather than a classic hotel suite. Natural materials, open-air structures and artisanal details root the design in the Mexican jungle and coast, while private plunge pools, outdoor showers, deep soaking tubs and broad decks make the tents feel expansive without overwhelming the landscape.

Cocina Copal is the central dining space, an open-air kitchen led by chef Sofía Mojica and shaped around local produce, mezcal, regional flavours and a flexible, all-inclusive rhythm. Meals may also take place in a bungalow, by the pool or on the beach, and the neighbouring Four Seasons resort broadens the choice with additional restaurants, bars, two golf courses, beaches, pools and spa facilities a short transfer away.

Wellness is integral rather than incidental. Two bamboo spa pods, a temazcal, forest bathing, sound rituals, yoga, nature hikes, snorkel safaris and water experiences draw directly from the setting. Low-impact construction, reclaimed and natural materials, onsite drinking-water production through SOURCE Water and careful protection of wildlife corridors reinforce Naviva’s unusually quiet, biophilic character. Seasonal whale sightings in Bahía de Banderas add another layer to the property’s deep connection with the Pacific coast.

highlights: Costalegre cliffside reserve with cinematic Pacific views, sustainable design and Elena Reygadas dining
description:
Four Seasons Resort Tamarindo occupies a secluded peninsula on Mexico’s Costalegre, between La Manzanilla and Barra de Navidad in Jalisco. The resort is set within a 3,000-acre private nature reserve where cliffs, jungle, coves and Pacific surf define the arrival, while Manzanillo-Costalegre airport places the property within practical reach without softening its remote coastal atmosphere.

The 157 rooms, suites, villas and beach houses are spread between cliffside and beachfront settings, with architecture by Víctor Legorreta and Mauricio Rocha and landscapes by Mario Schjetnan. Nature Rooms sit closer to the main resort, while suites may add private infinity pools, hammocks and outdoor showers. Larger villas and beach houses bring the same low-slung, landscape-led design to extended family stays.

The culinary programme is one of the resort’s strongest signatures. Coyul, developed in partnership with chef Elena Reygadas, centres on seasonality and sustainable Mexican ingredients, while Sal sits above Majahua Beach for seafood and sunset views. Nacho brings a more relaxed taqueria mood near the pool, and Rancho Lola, the resort’s low-impact farm, supports tree planting, cooking classes and farm-to-table meals.

Beyond the restaurants, the reserve is the defining amenity. The resort has a spa shaped by sea, jungle and ancestral Mexican rituals, pools, fitness facilities and an 18-hole, David Fleming-designed golf course with ocean views. Resident naturalists, ethnobotanical walks, macrophotography, hiking, seasonal whale-watching and family nature programming give the property a rare combination of polished resort comfort and genuine ecological immersion. Altogether, the property reads less as a beach resort inside a reserve than as a carefully choreographed encounter with the Costalegre landscape.

highlights: Lisbon grande dame with Art Deco poise, Tagus terraces and Michelin-starred CURA
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Lisbon rises beside Eduardo VII Park on Rua Rodrigo da Fonseca, just above Avenida da Liberdade and within easy reach of Marquês de Pombal, designer shopping, museum districts and the historic quarters below. Its hilltop position gives the hotel broad views across Old Lisbon, São Jorge Castle, the Tagus River and the 25 de Abril Bridge.

Known officially as Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon, the property remains one of the city’s defining grande dame hotels. Its 282 accommodations, including 242 rooms and 40 suites, combine private terraces in many categories with interiors that balance Art Deco geometry, Louis XVI references and a refreshed 1950s sensibility. Portuguese tapestries, paintings and sculpture fill the public spaces, making the hotel feel close to a private museum.

CURA is the culinary anchor, a one-Michelin-starred restaurant where chef Rodolfo Lavrador works with seasonal Portuguese ingredients and contemporary technique. The wider dining circuit includes Varanda, known for park-facing windows and weekend brunch, O Japonês, the Ritz Bar and the Almada Negreiros Lounge, where the hotel’s artistic heritage is particularly vivid.

Wellness carries the same urban polish. The spa has four treatment rooms, marble and oak detailing, a sauna and an 18-metre indoor pool overlooking the gardens, while a heated outdoor pool adds rare resort-like ease for central Lisbon. A rooftop fitness centre and running track frame cinematic city views, and curated art experiences and sidecar tours extend the hotel’s identity beyond its walls into Lisbon’s creative and historic streets. For a capital hotel, it delivers an unusually complete blend of heritage, gastronomy, art and urban resort-style leisure.
